title: Review: Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases; Strong and weak acids; Measuring rates; Collision theory and factors; Rate equations and orders
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AB03#t2 term and clue written for the game; AB01#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB03#t4 term and clue written for the game; AB01#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB01#N.6b, AB03#N.3b, KN01#N.3b, KN02#N.7b, KN04#N.3b, AB01#N.11, AB03#N.11, KN02#N.9a, AB01#N.10, AB03#N.7, AB03#N.4b. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Weak acid
items.clue: Its dissociation equilibrium lies far to the left, as with CH₃COOH.

items.label: Conjugate pair
items.clue: Two species that differ by exactly one proton, such as NH₄⁺ and NH₃.

items.label: Acid strength
items.clue: A measure of the extent of dissociation, not of how much is dissolved.

items.label: Amphiprotic
items.clue: Able to donate a proton or accept one, depending on its reaction partner.

questions.stem: The reaction HSO₄⁻(aq) + NH₃(aq) → SO₄²⁻(aq) + NH₄⁺(aq) occurs when the two species are mixed. Which choice gives the Brønsted–Lowry acid in the forward reaction, followed by its conjugate base?

options.text: HSO₄⁻, NH₃
HSO₄⁻, NH₄⁺
HSO₄⁻, SO₄²⁻
NH₃, NH₄⁺

questions.explanation: HSO₄⁻ gives a proton to NH₃, so it is the acid; what is left, SO₄²⁻, has one H fewer and one more negative charge: its conjugate base.

questions.stem: Two beakers at 25°C each contain 50 mL of an acid solution: one contains 0.10 M HCl(aq), and the other contains 0.10 M HA(aq), where HA is a weak monoprotic acid. Identical pieces of magnesium ribbon are dropped into the two beakers at the same moment. Which prediction about the first minute of the experiment is correct?

options.text: H₂ bubbles form at equal rates, because the two acid concentrations are equal
H₂ bubbles form faster in the HCl beaker, because its [H₃O⁺] is greater
H₂ bubbles form faster in the HA beaker, because it contains more acid molecules
No H₂ bubbles form in the HA beaker, because a weak acid does not ionize

questions.stem: Nitrogen and hydrogen react according to the equation N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g). Which statement correctly relates the rates at which the concentrations change while the reaction proceeds?

options.text: [N₂], [H₂] and [NH₃] change at the same rate.
[N₂] decreases three times as fast as [H₂] decreases.
[NH₃] increases two times as fast as [H₂] decreases.
[H₂] decreases three times as fast as [N₂] does.

questions.explanation: Three moles of H₂ react for every mole of N₂, so in any interval the change in [H₂] is three times the change in [N₂].

questions.stem: When a small amount of solid MnO₂ is added to a solution of hydrogen peroxide, H₂O₂(aq), bubbles of O₂(g) form rapidly as the H₂O₂ decomposes into H₂O and O₂. MnO₂ acts as a catalyst. Which statement about the MnO₂ is correct?

options.text: MnO₂ increases the total amount of O₂ that a sample of H₂O₂ can produce.
MnO₂ speeds up the decomposition and is not used up in the reaction.
MnO₂ is used up as it reacts, so its atoms end up as part of the products.
MnO₂ causes a decomposition of H₂O₂ that does not occur in its absence.

questions.explanation: A catalyst increases the rate without being used up overall, so the MnO₂ can be recovered at the end.

questions.stem: A hypothetical reaction is second order with respect to reactant A and first order with respect to reactant B. In a second trial at the same temperature, [A] is 4 times as great and [B] is 3 times as great as in the first trial. By what factor is the initial rate in the second trial greater than the initial rate in the first trial?
questions.explanation: With rate = k[A]²[B], the rate changes by 4² = 16 because of A and by 3 because of B: 16 × 3 = 48.

questions.stem: Water takes part in two reactions: (1) CH₃NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃NH₃⁺ + OH⁻ and (2) HBr + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Br⁻. What role does water play?

options.text: A base in (1) and an acid in (2)
An acid in both, as it releases H⁺ in each
Neither: it is neutral, so it is only the solvent
An acid in (1) and a base in (2)

questions.explanation: In (1) water donates H⁺ to the N lone pair of CH₃NH₂ and becomes OH⁻. In (2) it accepts H⁺ from HBr and becomes H₃O⁺. Water is amphiprotic: its role depends on its partner.

questions.stem: Which statement about solutions P and Q is correct? P is 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ M HCl(aq). Q is 0.50 M CH₃COOH(aq), measured pH 2.53.

options.text: P has the lower pH, as a strong acid always has a lower pH than a weak one.
P has the higher pH, even though HCl is the stronger acid.
CH₃COOH must be a strong acid, as Q has a lower pH than P.
HCl is a weak acid in P, as its concentration is low.

questions.explanation: P: pH = −log₁₀(5.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.30. Only about 1 in 170 CH₃COOH molecules in Q dissociates, but Q is 1000 times more concentrated, so [H⁺] ≈ 2.95 × 10⁻³, pH 2.53. pH depends on concentration as well as strength.

questions.stem: An iron nail held in a Bunsen flame only glows. The same mass of fine iron filings sprinkled into the flame burns in bright sparks. Why do the filings react so much faster with oxygen?

options.text: The filings are hotter than the nail, so their collisions with oxygen are more energetic.
Iron in small pieces has a lower activation energy for its reaction with oxygen.
The filings expose a far larger surface area, so collisions with oxygen are far more frequent.
The filings contain more iron atoms in total, so they release more energy.

questions.explanation: In a nail, most iron atoms are buried inside. In filings, far more atoms are on a surface, so many more successful collisions happen each second.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the hydrogensulfate ion, HSO₄⁻, acting as a Brønsted–Lowry acid?

options.text: HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂SO₄ + OH⁻
HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ SO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺
HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ SO₄²⁻ + H₃O⁺
HSO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂SO₄ + H₂O

questions.explanation: HSO₄⁻ loses one H⁺ to water, becoming SO₄²⁻. Losing a proton is what an acid does. Charges balance: −1 on each side.

questions.stem: Methanoic acid is a weak acid: HCOOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCOO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The equilibrium lies to the right, as all acids dissociate in water.
The equilibrium lies to the left, as HCOO⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O.
The equilibrium lies to the right, as HCOO⁻ is the weaker of the two bases.
The equilibrium lies to the left, as H₃O⁺ is a stronger acid than HCOOH.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium favours the weaker acid and weaker base. HCOOH is weaker than H₃O⁺, and H₂O weaker than HCOO⁻, so the left is favoured: few molecules dissociate.

questions.stem: Two solutions are prepared at 25°C: 0.10 M NH₃(aq), a weak base, and 0.10 M NaOH(aq). Which statement correctly compares the solutions?

options.text: [OH⁻] is equal in the two solutions, because each base ionizes completely in water
[OH⁻] is zero in the NH₃ solution, because NH₃ contains no OH group to release
[OH⁻] is lower in the NaOH solution, because NaOH stays mostly as NaOH units
[OH⁻] is lower in the NH₃ solution, because most NH₃ molecules remain un-ionized

questions.explanation: NaOH dissociates completely: [OH⁻] = 0.10 M. Only a small percentage of NH₃ molecules react with water, so [OH⁻] is much less than 0.10 M.
